response.description_long:
Data teams rarely find out a dashboard is wrong from a test suite. They find out in a QBR, when someone points at a number that shifted a quarter ago. Rowfern, a Denver company founded in 2022, is built around that specific failure mode: the company's pitch is testing and contract enforcement for data pipelines, catching broken schemas, silent nulls, and volume anomalies "in the pull request, not the postmortem."

The product starts by reading an existing dbt project or SQL pipelines and generating a suite of checks. Rather than testing tables in isolation, Rowfern parses dbt lineage to understand which models feed which, then generates schema contracts at the boundaries between producers and consumers — column names, types, nullability, accepted values. When a pull request changes a producing model, the contract check runs for every downstream consumer, so a column rename that would have silently nulled a marketing dashboard shows up as a red check listing the affected consumers. The author sees the blast radius before merge. Beyond schema, Rowfern learns freshness and volume expectations from history — how many rows a table gains on a normal Tuesday, how late its source usually lands — and recalibrates baselines as seasonality shifts, so a holiday dip doesn't page anyone. Hand-written YAML assertions cover business logic history can't learn: revenue is non-negative, every order has a customer, join keys are unique. Severity levels decide the consequence, from annotating a PR to blocking a merge to paging through PagerDuty or Slack using an ownership map pulled from dbt meta tags or a CODEOWNERS-style file.

The same checks that gate a pull request run on schedule in production, which the company describes as "one definition of correctness, enforced in both places." Alerts carry the failing check, the diff against baseline, and the downstream consumers. CI runs execute against a sampled snapshot of production data — enough rows to catch a fan-out or a type error, small enough to finish while review is still open, with typical runs completing under five minutes. Rowfern supports Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, and Databricks, running checks inside the customer's warehouse or over a read-only connection; sampled data does not leave the environment unless a customer opts into cloud snapshots. The company says it is SOC 2 Type II certified.

The business model is open core. The check engine — contract generator, check runner, CI integrations — is Apache 2.0 licensed and free forever for a single team on one project. The commercial platform adds the catalog of contracts, ownership routing, historical baselines computed from months of runs rather than days, SSO, audit logs, and an in-VPC read-only deployment. Cloud plans start at $500 per month per workspace, scaling with models under contract, with unlimited users and unlimited check runs; annual plans add SSO, audit logs, and the read-only deployment. The company frames the free engine as a funnel rather than leakage, noting that migration to a workspace imports existing configuration unchanged.

Named users are Chartbeam, Densify Analytics, and Copperline Health, which together run Rowfern on more than 4,000 models. Chartbeam gates every dbt PR on contracts and cites zero incidents traced to upstream schema changes for three consecutive quarters; Densify runs the open-source engine on two projects and the platform across the rest; Copperline Health, under healthcare compliance constraints, runs all checks in-warehouse with the read-only deployment. The company says teams typically adopt after a visible data outage — "a broken dashboard in a board meeting is a common origin story" — and the two founders, Owen Park and Talia Brooks, both former data engineers, include that experience in their own history. Rowfern employs 19 people, remote across US time zones, and maintains a public Slack with weekly office hours and a monthly changelog digest; the Databricks adapter reportedly began as a customer pull request.
